newsitem.title: UK: Britain's share market weighs up life under Labour.
newsitem.headline: Britain's share market weighs up life under Labour.

text.p: There are precedents for London's stock market to do well under a Labour government, despite the market's knee-jerk antipathy towards Labour, analysts say.

London's FTSE-index, which closed down 51 points, or 1.15 percent, on Monday, was less troubled by news that Prime Minister John Major had set May 1 as the election day than weakness on Wall Street, traders said.
The Labour party has a strong lead in opinion polls and a Labour victory has long been expected.

Worries over Labour policies, seen by the market as less friendly to business than those of the ruling Conservatives, have already overshadowed share prices for some months -- one reason the FTSE 100 has underperformed other leading European indexes this year.
But comparisons with past administrations may be fruitless since the world, and the Labour party, has changed hugely since the late 1970s when Labour was last in power.
For the equity market the central issue is likely to be Labour's overall handling of the economy and it is here that a key test is likely to come in the weeks after the election.

"Economic policies seem sane but it is so long since Labour was in power and that increases the uncertainty," said Ian Williams, strategist at Panmure Gordon. "All the talk could be irrelevant when they are in power."
Labour leader Tony Blair and his shadow finance minister Gordon Brown have worked hard to present a business-friendly front designed in part to keep the markets on their side.
In particular Labour has hinted that it will stick to the Conservatives' 2.5 percent inflation target and has said it will keep borrowing and taxes under control.
With economic growth poised to increase during 1997 while government debt remains high, the eventual victor may be faced with tough decisions to raise taxes and interest rates.

There are specific areas of tax policy that could have a significant bearing on shares. Labour is expected to introduce a multi-billion pound "windfall" tax on privatised utilities, designed to finance training and employment measures.

The party is expected to take a tougher line on takeovers, breaking the free market philosophy of recent years that has helped return billions of pounds for investment funds to reinvest in the market.
Another possibility is that Labour will introduce new shareholding rules to discourage over-active trading by investment funds in favour of long-term investment.

Whether Labour proves true to its promises remains to be seen, and much policy detail has still to be spelt out but investors seem reconciled to find ways to live with a Labour government after 18 years of Conservative rule.

Since the British stock market has not had to live with a Labour government for so long, its memories of the dying days of the last one are coloured by high inflation and strikes but a Leeds University study shows that life was not necessarily so bad for the market under Labour.
"If you adjust for statistical fluctuation there isn't any evidence that Labour has been any worse," said Robert Hudson, a research fellow at Leeds University's Centre for Financial Services.

Between Harold Wilson's Labour victory of October 1974 for instance and the re-election of the Conservatives under Margaret Thatcher in May 1979, the FT-All Share index quadrupled in value from just above 60 to over 280.

After the Wilson government's devaluation of early 1967, the index leapt from around 95 to end the year near 120. By contrast the bear market of 1973 and 1974 mostly occurred under the Conservative government of Edward Heath.
Such raw figures of course can be misleading, since they take no account of inflation or of the market's relative performance compared with other leading markets.
A more conventional view came from investment bank Robert Fleming, where analysts looked at the inflation-adjusted return from shares under different administrations since 1945.
Only between 1970 and 1974, a time when British industry was put on a three-day week to counter the effects of a coal miners' strike, was there a negative return under the Conservatives.
By comparison returns were negative under each period of Labour rule, Robert Fleming figures suggested.

"The lesson of history is slightly against being too optimistic on a Labour win," said Fleming chart analyst Chris Chaitow -- who pointed out that the market was anyway due a correction of perhaps 15 percent whoever wins the poll.

Yet some analysts believe the market will ride out any pre-election nerves. "My inclination is that if the market starts to get jumpy ahead of the election, if it overreacts in one way it will probably go the other way in the aftermath," said Williams at Panmure.
